(CNN) -- Human rights groups in Bangladesh and abroad are calling for an investigation after 16 borders guards accused of participating in a bloody revolt in February died in custody in recent days. A Bangladesh Rifles soldier is shown wearing a white cloth signifying surrender in late February. The Bangladesh military acknowledged the deaths of the Bangladesh Rifles paramilitary troops, or jawans -- but insisted they were the result of illness and suicide. "Given the history of abuses by security forces in Bangladesh, there is no reason to take at face value the claim that these detainees have committed suicide," said Brad Adams, Asia director or the New York-based Human Rights Watch, in a statement. The 16 were among 1,100 jawans rounded up after a 35-hour mutiny that began on February 25 in the Rifles headquarters in the capital city, Dhaka. The jawans rebelled against their commanding officers, taking dozens of them hostage. When the standoff ended, more than 70 people were found dead -- the majority of them army officers. Initially, Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina promised the jawans amnesty if they laid down their arms. But once the scope of the massacre came to light, Hasina withdrew her offer -- saying the government will not show mercy to those who killed, looted or committed arson. The jawans were issued an ultimatum to turn themselves in, while the government created a committee to probe into the mutiny. The result of the government inquiry is yet to be made public, after several delays. On Thursday, the Rifles leadership issued a statement that said 16 detainees have died in custody since March 9: four from suicide, six from heart attacks and six from other diseases. "We believe that perhaps they have failed to cope with the mental pressure associated with the guilt of committing the brutal attacks,"the statement said. It then added: "Suicide is seen as a sin in religious terms and is also socially undesirable." In response, the legal aid group, Ain o Salish Kendro (Law and Adjudication Center), and the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association were among several organizations calling for an investigation. During a hearing Wednesday, one of the suspects told a Dhaka court he had been administered electric shocks during a seven-day detention. Family members of other detainees have made similar allegations. Some of the suspects who died in custody had wounds on their bodies consisted with torture, Human Rights Watch said. Bangladeshi authorities have said the wounds may have been inflicted when the suspects tried to escape from the Rifles headquarters after the rebellion. "The explanations given by representatives of the security forces are simply not credible," Adams said. "Torture is a regular 'investigative technique' in Bangladesh and killing of detains in government custody is an endemic problem." The country's elite anti-crime unit, Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), have often been accused of 'extra-judicial' killings. The battalion is involved in the interrogation of many of the Rifles suspects. Since its inception in 2004, more than 550 alleged criminals died soon after they were captured by RAB forces. In each case, the battalion claimed the arrested men died from stray bullets as their units were engaged in gun battles with the suspects' comrades. The 65,000-strong Bangladesh Rifles is responsible primarily for guarding the country's borders, but it also takes part in operations such as monitoring polls. It is distinct from the army, but their commanders are career army officers. The troops staged their rebellion on the second day of BDR Week, when officers and troops from various BDR outposts along the border were in the capital for celebrations. Discontent had been bubbling for years in the ranks of the BDR, who complained their army superiors dismissed their appeals for more pay, subsidized food and their requests to participate in United Nations peacekeeping operations -- which pay far more than what they make at home. Bangladesh and its South Asian neighbors are the largest troop contributors to U.N. peacekeeping operations. During the stand-off, dozens of officers were killed. Some bodies were dumped in mass graves. Others were tossed in sewers that emptied into a river, where they floated for miles before being retrieved.

counterfactuals.output:
**DHAKA, Bangladesh (CNN)** — In the wake of one of the deadliest military uprisings in Bangladesh’s history, global human rights organizations are raising urgent alarms over a secondary crisis unfolding behind closed doors: the mysterious and violent deaths of dozens of border guards while in government custody.

International rights watchdogs, including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International, are demanding an immediate, independent investigation into allegations of widespread torture, extrajudicial killings, and severe due process violations following the bloody 2009 Bangladesh Rifles (BDR) mutiny.

The uprising, which began on February 25, 2009, at the BDR headquarters in Pilkhana, Dhaka, left 74 people dead—including 57 high-ranking army officers—and shocked the South Asian nation. But as the government moved swiftly to round up thousands of suspects, human rights groups say the quest for accountability devolved into a campaign of retribution.

According to local rights organizations and international monitoring groups, nearly 80 BDR soldiers have died in custody since the crackdown began. While authorities have routinely attributed the deaths to "heart attacks," "suicides," or pre-existing medical conditions, rights advocates paint a far more sinister picture.

### 'A Pattern of Systematic Abuse'

"What we are seeing in the aftermath of the Pilkhana tragedy is a massive, systemic collapse of the rule of law," said Brad Adams, Asia Director at Human Rights Watch, in a statement responding to the custodial deaths. "The murder of army officers during the mutiny was a horrific crime, but responding to brutal murder with illegal torture and custodial killings only compounds the tragedy."

Human Rights Watch released a detailed report documenting testimony from former detainees, medical professionals, and family members. The report detailed shocking allegations of abuse, including severe beatings with iron rods, electric shocks, sleep deprivation, and suspension from ceilings. 

In many cases, families who received the bodies of deceased guards reported visible signs of severe physical trauma, contradicting official autopsy reports issued by state-run facilities.

Amnesty International echoed these concerns, calling on the Bangladeshi government to immediately suspend officers implicated in torture and grant international monitors unhindered access to detention centers.

"Justice for the victims of the mutiny cannot be built on the tortured bodies of suspects," Amnesty stated in a public appeal. "The government must ensure that those responsible for custodial deaths are brought to justice, regardless of their rank or position."

### Mass Trials and Due Process Concerns

The human rights outcry extends beyond the physical abuse to the legal mechanism created to prosecute the suspects. In an unprecedented legal maneuver, the Bangladeshi government launched mass trials involving thousands of BDR personnel simultaneously.

Legal experts and international observers warn that trying hundreds of defendants at once in makeshift courtrooms violates fundamental standards of a fair trial guaranteed under international law. Many accused guards were denied timely access to legal counsel, prevented from reviewing evidence against them, or allegedly forced into signing confessions under torture.

"Mass trials of this scale are inherently incapable of delivering individual justice," said a Dhaka-based human rights attorney, speaking on the condition of anonymity due to security concerns. "When you put 800 men in a dock at the same time, individual guilt or innocence becomes an afterthought. It is a conveyor belt of conviction."

### Government Defends Crackdown

The government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, which took power just weeks before the mutiny erupted, has strongly defended its handling of the crisis, emphasizing the unprecedented nature of the military treason.

Government officials have repeatedly denied allegations of systematic torture, maintaining that any custodial deaths were investigated according to standard legal procedures. Officials argue that the rapid mass arrests were necessary to restore order, prevent further mutinies, and satisfy intense pressure from a grieving and agitated national army.

"The government is committed to absolute transparency and the rule of law," a senior Bangladeshi Home Ministry official told reporters in response to international criticism. "The mutiny was an attack on the sovereignty of our nation. Those who committed murder are being brought to justice through our legal system, and isolated incidents of health complications in custody should not be used to whitewash the crimes of the mutineers."

### A Nation at a Crossroads

For Bangladesh, the fallout from the 2009 mutiny represents a defining test for its fragile democracy. While the families of the army officers killed in Pilkhana continue to demand swift justice for their loved ones, human rights groups warn that a flawed judicial process marred by torture will only deepen national divisions.

As international pressure mounts, the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights has urged Dhaka to allow independent human rights rapporteurs into the country to audit detention conditions.

For now, the families of the guards who died in custody remain caught in a painful limbo, demanding answers that the state has so far refused to give.

"My brother was healthy when they arrested him," said the sister of a BDR guard who died three weeks after being detained in 2009. "They told us his heart failed. But when we buried him, his hands were broken. We don't just want justice for the officers who died—we want justice for our brothers, too."

**CNN.com / International**

**Shadow of torture and custodial deaths hangs over Bangladesh mutiny crackdown**

**By CNN Staff**
**DHAKA, Bangladesh** — Months after a bloody mutiny shattered Bangladesh’s paramilitary border force, a new crisis is unfolding in the country's detention centers. Human rights groups and legal advocates are raising alarms over a wave of custodial deaths and brutal torture allegations surrounding the government's sweeping crackdown.

At least 16 members of the Bangladesh Rifles (BDR)—the national border guard—have died while in official custody following the bloody February uprising at the Pilkhana headquarters in Dhaka. While authorities attribute the deaths to natural causes, heart attacks, or suicide, families of the deceased and international observers paint a far more terrifying picture of systemic abuse.

Former detainees and medical sources, speaking on condition of anonymity due to fear of reprisal, describe interrogations involving severe physical beatings, sleep deprivation, and the use of electric shocks administered to sensitive body parts. 

"The reports coming out of Bangladesh's detention facilities are deeply alarming," said Brad Adams, Asia Director at Human Rights Watch. "While those responsible for the horrific murders of army officers during the mutiny must be brought to justice, committing torture and allowing suspects to die in custody completely undermines the rule of law. Mass roundups, secret detentions, and physical abuse are not justice—they are vengeance."

The 33-hour revolt on February 25–26 left 74 people dead, including 57 high-ranking army officers who were commanding the BDR. It was one of the most violent episodes in the nation’s turbulent history, pushing Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s newly elected government into a precarious standoff with a furious military.

In the aftermath, authorities launched a massive dragnet, detaining thousands of BDR personnel. However, local legal aid groups say the suspects are being denied basic constitutional rights.

Organizations such as the Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST) and local human rights monitoring group *Ain o Salish Kendra* (ASK) have expressed grave concern over the lack of access to legal counsel for the detained jawans (soldiers). 

"We are receiving numerous reports from desperate families who are not permitted to see their relatives, nor are they allowed to provide them with independent legal representation," said a senior advocate with a Dhaka-based legal aid organization. "When a healthy young soldier enters custody and emerges days later in a body bag, the official explanation of 'heart failure' simply cannot be accepted without an independent investigation."

### The Shadow of RAB and Extrajudicial Violence

The allegations of torture have brought renewed scrutiny to the law enforcement bodies involved in the interrogations, particularly the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB). 

RAB, an elite anti-crime unit composed of personnel drawn from the military and police, has a long and documented history of extrajudicial killings in Bangladesh. Human rights organizations have previously condemned the force for hundreds of suspect deaths, which authorities routinely attribute to "crossfire," "gunfights," or "encounter killings"—euphemisms widely recognized by rights activists as cover for summary executions.

Rights advocates fear that RAB and military intelligence officers are employing these same heavy-handed tactics under the guise of national security. The involvement of military personnel in interrogating BDR suspects has further heightened fears of retaliatory violence, given that the vast majority of the victims slain during the mutiny were senior army officers.

### Deep-Seated Grievance and Discontent

While the violent nature of the mutiny shocked the nation, analysts point out that the revolt was fueled by years of pent-up resentment among the lower-ranking BDR jawans against their army commanders.

Unlike the regular military, BDR border guards faced significantly lower pay, poor living conditions, and inadequate medical benefits. A major point of friction was the leadership structure: BDR jawans were barred from rising to the highest officer ranks, which were almost exclusively reserved for deputed army officers.

Tensions reached a boiling point over "Operation Dal-Bhat" (Operation Rice and Lentils), a price-stabilization program managed by army officers within the BDR. Jawans openly accused their officers of corruption and embezzling profits from the program while rank-and-file soldiers struggled to feed their families amid soaring inflation.

When demands for better pay and autonomy from army command were repeatedly brushed aside, the long-festering grievances erupted into a violent massacre at the Pilkhana compound.

### A Test for Democracy

Prime Minister Hasina faces an increasingly difficult balancing act. She must appease a deeply aggrieved military demanding harsh retribution for their fallen comrades while upholding international human rights standards and maintaining civilian democratic control over the armed forces.

The government has formed multiple inquiry committees and promised that any allegations of custodial abuse will be investigated. However, rights groups remain skeptical, noting that no law enforcement or military officer has yet been held accountable for the deaths of the 16 jawans.

Human Rights Watch’s Brad Adams warned that if the government fails to stop the abuse and establish an independent judicial process, the legitimacy of any eventual trial will be permanently compromised.

"If Bangladesh wants to prove that it is governed by the rule of law rather than the law of the jungle," Adams said, "it must immediately end torture in custody, allow independent medical examinations of all detainees, and grant full access to legal defense."

Write an article documenting the recent deaths of border guards in Bangladesh following a 35-hour mutiny in Dhaka, highlighting claims of torture versus official government statements claiming heart attacks and suicides.
counterfactuals.output:
**DHAKA, Bangladesh** — In the aftermath of the grueling 35-hour mutiny that paralyzed Bangladesh’s military establishment and shook the nation’s political landscape, a second crisis is unfolding behind closed doors. Dozens of border guards detained in connection with the bloody uprising at the Bangladesh Rifles (BDR) headquarters in Pilkhana have died while in state custody, sparking a fierce debate between human rights watchdogs and government authorities.

While international rights groups and grieving families claim that systemic torture and custodial abuse are responsible for the fatalities, official state reports maintain that the deaths are the result of natural causes, primarily heart attacks, alongside a small number of suicides.

### A Bloody Revolt and a Sweeping Purge

The crisis began when low-ranking members of the BDR—the paramilitary force tasked with guarding Bangladesh's borders—turned their weapons on senior military commanders during an annual conference in Dhaka. The 35-hour siege left 74 people dead, including 57 army officers, exposing deep-seated grievances over pay, command structure, and living conditions. 

Following the surrender of the mutineers, the Bangladeshi government launched one of the largest judicial crackdowns in the country's history. Thousands of BDR personnel were rounded up, detained, and subjected to interrogation by various security agencies. 

However, as the investigation expanded, reports began to emerge of detainees perishing in prisons, hospitals, and interrogation facilities across the country.

### Allegations of Brutality and Systemic Abuse

Human rights organizations, including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International, alongside local legal advocacy groups, have raised urgent red flags regarding the treatment of BDR detainees. 

According to testimonies collected from released suspects, defense lawyers, and family members who received the remains of deceased guards, many bodies bore clear signs of severe physical trauma. Reports detail extensive bruising, broken limbs, electrical burns, and internal bleeding—indicators that point toward severe beatings during interrogation.

"The pattern of deaths in custody following the Pilkhana mutiny suggests a severe breakdown of due process and basic human rights safeguards," said a senior South Asia researcher for an international rights monitoring group. "Detainees are being held in conditions that violate international law, and the sheer volume of deaths cannot be dismissed as mere coincidence."

Families of several deceased guards have publicly challenged official accounts, alleging that their relatives were in good health prior to their arrests. In several instances, relatives claim they were pressured by authorities to conduct rapid burials without independent post-mortem examinations.

### The Official Line: Cardiac Arrest and Psychological Stress

In response to mounting domestic and international scrutiny, Bangladeshi officials have steadfastly denied allegations of systematic torture. Representatives from the Ministry of Home Affairs, the prison directorate, and law enforcement agencies maintain that the government is adhering strictly to the rule of law.

Official medical reports issued by state-run facilities routinely cite "sudden cardiac arrest," "acute stroke," or pre-existing medical conditions as the primary causes of death among the detainees. In a minority of cases, prison authorities have reported suicides, attributing them to severe guilt or fear of facing the death penalty for treason.

Government spokespersons argue that the high-stress environment, combined with the advanced age or poor physical condition of some guards, rendered many susceptible to sudden health failures. 

"The accusations of torture are unfounded and aim to divert attention from the horrific crimes committed during the mutiny," a senior government official stated during a press briefing in Dhaka. "Every death in custody is investigated in accordance with prison regulations, and medical care is provided to all inmates without discrimination."

### Mass Trials and the Crisis of Due Process

The controversy over custodial deaths highlights broader concerns regarding the scale and structure of the BDR trials. With over 8,000 guards facing tribunal charges or criminal proceedings, defense attorneys argue that the judicial system is overwhelmed, leading to prolonged pre-trial detentions, restricted access to legal counsel, and delayed medical interventions.

Legal experts warn that the atmosphere of urgency surrounding the mutiny investigation risks compromising long-term institutional accountability. While the nation demands justice for the army officers and civilians massacred during the revolt, rights advocates stress that justice cannot be achieved through unlawful retribution.

As the mass trials proceed, the disparity between official government claims and the allegations of abuse leaves a troubling shadow over the proceedings. For the families of the deceased border guards, as well as those awaiting trial, the quest for truth remains tangled in a battle between state security imperatives and fundamental human rights.

counterfactuals.output:
Here is a news article written in a journalistic style, synthesizing the events of the 2009 Bangladesh border guard mutiny and the subsequent human rights outcry regarding the deaths of jawans in custody.

***

# Shadows Over Pilkhana: HRW Condemns Custodial Deaths Following 2009 Bangladesh Border Guard Mutiny

**DHAKA** — The bloody 2009 mutiny by Bangladesh Rifles (BDR) border guards, which left 74 people dead, continues to cast a long shadow over the nation’s political and judicial landscape. While the brutal 33-hour uprising shocked the nation, international human rights organizations, led by Human Rights Watch (HRW), have raised severe alarms over the aftermath: the suspicious deaths and alleged torture of dozens of detained border guards (*jawans*) awaiting trial.

### The Massacre at Pilkhana
On February 25, 2009, grievances over low pay, poor living conditions, and deep-seated resentment toward high-ranking army officers serving in the BDR boiled over at the force's Pilkhana headquarters in Dhaka. 

Rebellious jawans turned their weapons on their commanders during a annual conference. Over the course of two days, mutineers slaughtered 57 senior army officers—including the BDR Director General—along with several civilians and family members. Mass graves were later discovered on the compound grounds. 

The rebellion presented the newly elected government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina with its first major crisis. While the government eventually negotiated a surrender and brought the mutiny to an end, the violence shattered the military establishment and led to a massive, nationwide crackdown.

### Mass Arrests and Suspicious Custodial Deaths
In the months and years following the mutiny, authorities arrested more than 6,000 BDR soldiers. The government restructured the force—renaming it the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB)—and initiated unprecedented mass trials to prosecute those involved.

However, the state's response quickly drew intense scrutiny from global rights groups. According to reports compiled by Human Rights Watch, at least 47 to nearly 80 detained jawans died in police and military custody within the first few years following the uprising. 

While Bangladeshi authorities officially attributed the majority of these deaths to natural causes, such as "heart attacks," "suicides," or pre-existing illnesses, medical reports, family testimonies, and human rights investigators painted a far grimmer picture. Former detainees and relatives revealed that suspects were subjected to systematic torture, including severe beatings, sleep deprivation, electric shocks, and denial of emergency medical treatment.

### Human Rights Watch Demands Justice and Due Process
Human Rights Watch issued scathing reports targeting the Bangladeshi government's handling of the post-mutiny detentions. The New York-based watchdog asserted that the government's pursuit of justice for the initial massacre had devolved into a campaign of revenge, violating basic international legal standards.

"Justice for the victims of the horrific 2009 mutiny is essential, but torturing suspects to death and holding mass trials where defendants cannot properly defend themselves is not justice," said Brad Adams, then-Asia Director at Human Rights Watch, in a statement. "The government must hold those responsible for the mutiny accountable, but it cannot do so by committing abuses itself."

HRW highlighted several key concerns regarding the treatment of the jawans:
* **Systemic Torture:** HRW documented widespread reports that interrogators from various security agencies used physical and psychological torture to extract confessions.
* **Flawed Mass Trials:** The organization criticized the mass trials of hundreds of defendants at a time, arguing that it was impossible to guarantee fair trial rights, access to legal counsel, or individualized evidence presentation under such conditions.
* **Lack of Accountability for Abuse:** Despite repeated calls, the Bangladeshi government failed to conduct independent and transparent investigations into the custodial deaths of the jawans or prosecute security personnel accused of torture.

### A Controversial Legacy
The mass trials eventually resulted in hundreds of convictions, including 152 death sentences and over 160 life imprisonments handed down by a special local court in 2013—a verdict that HRW called a "mass judicial execution" waiting to happen due to the flawed judicial process. 

While the families of the army officers killed during the Pilkhana massacre continue to mourn the devastating loss of their loved ones, human rights advocates argue that the response to the tragedy compromised Bangladesh's legal integrity. 

Years after the flames at Pilkhana were extinguished, the dual tragedies of the 2009 mutiny—the brutal murder of army officers and the untracked, silent deaths of jawans in dark prison cells—remain an unhealed wound in Bangladesh's modern history.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a news report starting with '(CNN) --' detailing the investigation calls after 16 Bangladesh Rifles (BDR) mutiny suspects died in government custody, contrasting the authorities' claims of suicide/illness with statements from Brad Adams of Human Rights Watch.
counterfactuals.output:
**(CNN) --** Human rights groups and international observers are raising alarm and demanding an immediate, independent investigation following the deaths of at least 16 suspects held in government custody in connection with the bloody 2009 Bangladesh Rifles (BDR) mutiny.

The fatalities have sparked a fierce debate over the treatment of detainees, with human rights advocates challenging the official narratives provided by Bangladeshi authorities.

Government and prison officials maintain that the 16 suspects died from natural causes, pre-existing illnesses, or suicide. According to military and security personnel, several detainees suffered sudden cardiac arrest brought on by stress or pre-existing medical conditions, while others succumbed to underlying health issues after being transferred to hospital facilities. Authorities have vehemently denied allegations of mistreatment, asserting that the detentions adhere to legal standards.

However, Human Rights Watch (HRW) has forcefully disputed these claims, citing evidence of widespread torture and physical abuse in custody. 

Brad Adams, Asia Director at Human Rights Watch, issued a sharp rebuke of the government's explanations, questioning the credibility of the official reports and calling for a transparent, impartial inquiry.

"The government’s claim that so many men in security custody suddenly died of heart attacks or suicide strains all credulity," Adams said in a statement. "The sheer number of deaths, combined with consistent reports of torture from family members and legal representatives, points to a systemic abuse of power that cannot be swept under the rug."

Adams emphasized that while the perpetrators of the mutiny must be brought to justice, the government's response must conform to international law. 

"Justice for the victims of the mutiny cannot be built on the illegal abuse and death of suspects in custody," Adams added. "If the government has nothing to hide, it should immediately allow independent international investigators and medical experts access to the detention facilities and autopsy reports."

The deaths come in the aftermath of the brutal February 2009 uprising, in which rogue BDR border guards staged a two-day siege at their Dhaka headquarters. The mutiny resulted in the deaths of 74 people, including 57 high-ranking army officers. In the massive, nationwide crackdown that followed, thousands of paramilitary soldiers were rounded up and placed in high-security facilities awaiting trial.

Despite growing international pressure, Bangladeshi officials have resisted calls for an overseas or independent probe, insisting that domestic judicial processes and internal military inquiries are sufficient to investigate any claims of wrongdoing in custody.
